title: Shop Divider
context: Grade 4, the chapter's recap and the dividing half of its last section. An adult sees shopping sums. What is actually being settled is what each division answers. Dividing a total cost by the number of things gives the cost of one, which is money. Dividing money by the price of one gives how many can be bought, which is a number of things, and the remainder is money too little for one more. The closing ticket table asks for the price of one ticket and then the total spent, which adds what was spent and not one ticket from each row. Every division in the chapter divides a whole number of rupees, and this tool divides nothing else.

writeup.why: Divide whole rupees to find the cost of one or how many can be bought, keep the money left over, and give every answer in the unit the question asks for.
writeup.look: A shop counter with a till on the left and a shelf on the right, a question card at the top, and a share mat and a buy lane between them.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Shop Divider' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: on the first phase the piles filled against the things the total is shared among, and on the second the rows priced against the rows of the table, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each pile or row is done and the second fixed at what this phase holds. On the third and fourth phases it carries the things paid for alone, one number climbing by one as the lane pays out each price, with no second number beside it, because how many is the question being asked. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The question card runs across the top of the working area, 1086 by 76 at 64,214, saying what is known and what is asked, with its last words, the thing asked for, underlined in near-black. The till stands at the left, 260 by 420 at 64,302, holding a whole number of rupees as play notes and coins sorted by value, with its amount written under it in deep blue. The share mat stands beside it, 520 by 250 at 340,302, laying out as many empty piles as there are things, in rows of up to six, and dealing the till's money onto them a round at a time, changing a note for smaller notes and coins of the same total whenever the notes will not go round, until every pile holds the same; one pile's amount is written under it in deep blue. The division frame stands at the right, 280 by 250 at 870,302, writing the same division in full, one digit brought down at a time, its quotient in deep blue when it is money and in sky blue when it counts things. On the second phase a ticket table replaces the mat and the frame, 810 by 250 at 340,302: a row for each group of tickets, with columns for tickets bought, amount spent and price of one ticket, the last blank until it is found, and a total line under the amount spent column only. Tapping a row opens the share mat over the table for that row alone. The buy lane runs along the foot, 620 by 150 at 340,570: a price tag at its left, and the things paid for standing in a counted row beside it in rows of ten. Each tap pays the price out of the till into the lane and sets one thing on the shelf, and the lane stops when what is left in the till is less than the price. The money left tray sits at the right end of the lane, 180 by 150 at 970,570, holding what the lane could not spend, written under it in reddish purple. A check control on the tray multiplies back and adds the money left. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across, with a unit strip under it reading rupees and things, and the answer slot will not close on a number whose unit is not the one the question asks for. On the fourth phase the slot is split in two, the left half marked things in sky blue and the right half marked rupees left in reddish purple, and each half takes its own number. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own and are the pictures' colours too. The rupees of every amount, the rupees column and the value printed on every note and coin are deep blue. The paise of every amount, the paise column and every cell standing for paise are green. The dot between rupees and paise is vermilion, a clear round dot, and wherever amounts stand in columns it sits on a near-black dotted line. A rupee carried from the paise, and a rupee broken into a hundred paise with the digits it rewrites, are amber. The change handed back, the money left and a remainder are reddish purple, so money coming back is never mistaken for a cost. A count of things, a number multiplied by, how many notes of one value or how many can be bought, is sky blue, because a count of things is not money. The zeros that fill the paise column of a whole-rupee amount in column working are grey. Every play note is one plain pale blue rectangle and every play coin one plain steel disc, all notes one size and all coins one size, each printed with its value and nothing else. No coin below one rupee is drawn anywhere: paise are shaded cells on a strip ruled into a hundred in ten blocks of ten, so a full strip is exactly one rupee. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome: every column rule, dotted line, tick, bracket, strike line, bill rule and panel edge is near-black. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a digit is told apart by the column it stands in, a carry by the circle it sits in, a count by the box beside the times sign or the slot marked things, and the change or money left by the tray or line that holds it, before any of them is told by a colour. Grey never means faint: a zero in a paise column is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and is never dimmed, shrunk or left out. A rupees figure that goes down by one is struck through once with the new figure written above it, and never rubbed out. Every amount in the till is a whole number of rupees, because every division in this chapter divides whole rupees, and on the first two phases every total shares out exactly among its things, so no pile is ever asked to hold paise. The unit printed in the answer slot is the unit the question card's last words ask for, and it does not change to fit an answer.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last division the child worked, its answer in the unit the question asked for, and the check that multiplies back to the money in the till.

phases.win: every pile holds the same amount, and the frame's answer matches one pile, in rupees
phases.does: shares the total into as many equal piles as there are things, then works the division in the frame and reads one pile
phases.goal: when each thing costs the same, the cost of one is the total cost divided by the number of things
phases.says: The total cost is shared among the things. What does one cost?
phases.check: Away from the screen: eight torches cost Rs 736. What does one torch cost? Say the unit.
phases.feels: the total is dealt out fairly, and one share is the price of one thing
phases.hands: Put Rs 96 of play money on a desk, a fifty rupee note, two twenty rupee notes and six one rupee coins, and say it is the cost of four toys that each cost the same. A child deals it onto four plates, changing notes for smaller ones when they will not go round, until every plate holds the same. Ask whether one plate is rupees or toys.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: how many things share the total? Second rung, the phase's: what does one pile hold? Third rung: the mat is cut to a total of twenty rupees shared among four things, and the child deals it before the larger total comes back. The number pad and the unit strip stay open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: a price and a number of things stand in the question together, and multiplying a price by a number of things is the move just practised.
wrong.move: multiplies Rs 522 by six and writes Rs 3132, which is the cost of thirty-six lunch boxes, not one.
wrong.screen: the share mat lays out six piles and deals the till's Rs 522 onto them until each holds eighty-seven rupees. The child's Rs 3132 is set beside the till, and the frame shows what it is: the cost of thirty-six lunch boxes at eighty-seven rupees each. The child's number stays in the slot.

wrong.why: the question talks about lunch boxes, and the frame's answer is a bare number with nothing to say what it counts.
wrong.move: writes eighty-seven lunch boxes, giving the cost of one as a number of things.
wrong.screen: the unit strip under the slot lights rupees, the unit the question card's last words ask for, and one pile on the mat is lit with its amount under it in deep blue, eighty-seven rupees in notes and coins. The frame's quotient turns deep blue, money, and the child's eighty-seven stays in the slot.

phases.screen: a question card giving a number of things and their total cost, with the share mat and the frame empty
phases.soWhat: When each thing costs the same, the cost of one is the total cost divided by the number of things.

phases.win: each price settles in its row, and the total spent lands under the amounts spent, not under the prices
phases.does: divides each row's amount spent by its tickets, writes the price of one, then adds the amounts spent for the total
phases.goal: the price of one ticket is the amount spent divided by the number of tickets, and the total spent adds what was spent
phases.says: Is the price of one ticket the same as the amount spent?
phases.check: Five tickets cost Rs 435. What is the price of one ticket, and what was spent?
phases.feels: the amount spent paid for every ticket in the row, and one ticket is one share of it
phases.hands: Make flashcards for the chapter's six vocabulary words, with a plain meaning on the back of each, such as: a bill lists the things bought and their prices, and cost is the price to be paid. Then draw a ticket table on the board with two rows, tickets bought and amount spent, and a blank column headed price of one ticket. Fill the column by dividing, and ask what the total spent should add.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many tickets did this row buy? Second rung, the phase's: is the price of one ticket the amount spent? Third rung: the table is cut to one row of two tickets for sixty rupees, and the child finds one ticket's price before the other rows come back. The number pad and the unit strip stay open.

wrong.why: the amount spent is the only money printed in the row, so it looks like the price.
wrong.move: gives the amount spent in a row, Rs 858, as the price of one ticket.
wrong.screen: the share mat opens over the row and deals its Rs 858 into six piles, one for each ticket bought, and every pile holds one hundred and forty-three rupees. That amount settles in the price column, and the child's Rs 858 stays in the slot.

wrong.why: the prices were just found and are the newest numbers in the table, so adding them looks like the next step.
wrong.move: adds one ticket from each row, Rs 143 and Rs 70, and calls Rs 213 the total spent.
wrong.screen: the total line lights under the amount spent column, not under the prices, and the two amounts spent slide down into it: Rs 858 and Rs 560 make Rs 1418. The child's Rs 213 is shown for what it is, the cost of one ticket from each row, two tickets where fourteen were bought, and it stays in the slot.

phases.screen: a ticket table with the tickets bought and the amount spent in each row, and the price column blank
phases.soWhat: The price of one ticket is the amount spent divided by the tickets; the total spent adds the amounts spent.

phases.win: the row of things stands complete, and its count lands in the answer slot marked things
phases.does: pays the price out again and again, or divides in the frame, and counts the things bought
phases.goal: how many things an amount buys is the money divided by the price of one, and the answer is a number of things
phases.says: The answer is a number of what, rupees or things?
phases.check: A balloon costs Rs 6. How many can be bought for Rs 138? Say the unit.
phases.feels: each payment buys one thing, so counting the payments counts the things
phases.hands: Price a sticker at Rs 4 and give a pair Rs 48 in play money. One pays four rupees at a time to the shopkeeper while the other lines up a sticker for each payment. Count the stickers, then write forty-eight divided by four, and ask what the twelve counts.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what is the price of one? Second rung, the phase's: is the answer rupees or things? Third rung: the till is cut to twenty rupees and a price of five, and the child pays it out one thing at a time before the larger amount comes back. The number pad and the unit strip stay open.

wrong.why: the division was worked on rupees, so its answer seems to be rupees too.
wrong.move: writes Rs 163, as if the number of notebooks were money.
wrong.screen: the unit strip under the slot lights things, the unit the question card's last words ask for, and the frame's quotient turns sky blue. The lane pays nine rupees out for each notebook, first at walking pace and then ten at a time, and the notebooks stand on the shelf in rows of ten, sixteen full rows and three more, with nothing left in the till. The child's Rs 163 stays in the slot.

wrong.why: there is an amount of money and a price in the question, and multiplying by a price is how the cost of many was found.
wrong.move: multiplies Rs 1467 by the price of nine and writes thirteen thousand two hundred and three notebooks.
wrong.screen: the lane pays out nine rupees for each notebook, and the child's number is set beside the till: each notebook costs nine rupees, so there cannot be more notebooks than rupees, and the till holds only one thousand four hundred and sixty-seven. The frame then divides, and the child's number stays in the slot.

phases.screen: a price tag, the till holding an amount, and an empty row on the shelf
phases.soWhat: How many things an amount buys is the money divided by the price of one, and the answer counts things.

phases.win: both slots fill, and the things times the price, with the money left added, rebuild the money in the till
phases.does: divides, puts the quotient in the things slot and the remainder in the money slot, then multiplies back and adds to check
phases.goal: the remainder is the money left over, too little to buy one more
phases.says: Some money is left. Is it enough for one more?
phases.check: Mangoes cost Rs 9 each. How many can be bought for Rs 100, and how much is left?
phases.feels: the rupees left are real money, just too few to buy another
phases.hands: Price a pencil at Rs 6 and give a pair Rs 45 in play money. They buy pencils six rupees at a time until they cannot buy another, then count the pencils and the rupees left. Write forty-five divided by six, and ask which number is pencils and which is money.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how much is left in the till? Second rung, the phase's: is that enough for one more? Third rung: the till is cut to seventeen rupees and a price of five, and the child pays out until the lane stops before the larger amount comes back. The number pad and both halves of the slot stay open.

wrong.why: the quotient answers the first question, and a single rupee looks too small to count as an answer.
wrong.move: writes two hundred and sixty-six pencils and stops, dropping the one rupee left.
wrong.screen: the right half of the split slot, rupees left, lights in reddish purple beside the child's answer, and the money left tray is lit with one rupee coin in it. The check runs: six times two hundred and sixty-six is one thousand five hundred and ninety-six, and the one rupee left makes one thousand five hundred and ninety-seven. The child's answer stays in the slot.

wrong.why: something is left over, and it feels like the start of one more pencil.
wrong.move: counts the rupee left as one more pencil and writes two hundred and sixty-seven.
wrong.screen: the lane tries to pay six rupees for one more pencil and finds one rupee in the till, and the price tag lights beside it, six against one. No pencil is set on the shelf, the rupee stays in the money left tray, and the child's two hundred and sixty-seven stays in the slot.

phases.screen: a till whose amount does not divide exactly by the price, with one slot for things and one for money left
phases.soWhat: In a how-many division, the remainder is the money left over, too little to buy one more.

writeup.delight: The fourth phase, the moment the check control runs. Every thing on the shelf turns back into its price, one after another, each price flying back into the till, and last the money left tips in from its tray. The till fills to exactly the amount it began with, not a rupee over and not a rupee short, and its amount under it lights. It can be run as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the question card gives a number of things and their total cost, the till holds that total, and the share mat and the division frame stand empty. On the second the ticket table stands in the mat's place, rows of tickets bought and amounts spent with the price column blank and the total line empty. On the third a price tag stands at the head of the buy lane, the till holds the money and the row on the shelf is empty. On the fourth the till holds an amount the price will not divide exactly, and the answer slot is split in two, things and rupees left. The running count at the top left holds the piles or rows done, or the things paid for, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the question card's last words, or the blank price column, or the price tag, or the split slot, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks what the question is asking for. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any whole-rupee amount and any price, with the share mat, the buy lane and the ticket table open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on the cost of one, the price of one ticket, how many can be bought, and the money left over.
voiceLines: A till of rupees and a shelf of things. What is the question asking for?
The total cost is shared among the things. What does one cost?
Is the price of one ticket the same as the amount spent?
The answer is a number of what, rupees or things?
Some money is left. Is it enough for one more?
A new question. Say what the answer counts before you divide.
Free play. Any whole rupee amount and any price, with the mat, the lane and the table open.
Read the question card again. Is the answer rupees, or things?
Every cost of one found, every count of things given, and every rupee left kept.

observations.why: The total cost was shared equally among the things, so one pile is what one thing costs.
observations.soWhat: When each thing costs the same, the cost of one is the total cost divided by the number of things.
observations.observe: Every pile held the same amount, and one pile matched the frame's answer, in rupees.

observations.why: The amount spent in a row paid for all its tickets, and the total spent adds what every row paid.
observations.soWhat: The price of one ticket is the amount spent divided by the tickets; the total spent adds the amounts spent.
observations.observe: Each price of one ticket settled in its row, and the total spent landed under the amounts spent.

observations.why: Each payment buys one thing, so the number of payments is the number of things.
observations.soWhat: How many things an amount buys is the money divided by the price of one, and the answer counts things.
observations.observe: The lane paid the price out once for each thing on the shelf, and the count landed in the slot marked things.

observations.why: The remainder is money that is too little to buy another thing.
observations.soWhat: In a how-many division, the remainder is the money left over, too little to buy one more.
observations.observe: What stayed in the tray was less than the price, and the lane would not pay for one more.

source_tool.description: A shop counter fills the stage, with a till of whole-rupee notes and coins on the left and a shelf of things on the right. A question card at the top says what is known and what is asked. A share mat splits an amount of money into equal piles, one pile for each thing, and a division frame beside it writes the same division in full, so the cost of one is read off a pile. A ticket table holds rows of tickets bought and amounts spent, a blank price column, and a total line under the amounts spent. A buy lane works the other way round: the price of one is set on a tag, and the till pays that price out again and again, one thing at a time, until what is left is too little for one more. The things bought stand in a counted row, and the money left stays in the till tray, labelled in rupees. An answer slot at the right carries the unit the question asks for: rupees for a cost or the money left, and things for how many. Every amount on the till is a whole number of rupees, because every division in this chapter divides whole rupees.
source_tool.art_direction: A till, a shelf and equal piles / Picture book

audio.note: Web Audio oscillators, no files. The same three cues in every tool of every Class 4 chapter, so the grade sounds like one grade.

wrong.note: A soft low double-bloop. A nudge, never a buzzer.

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a rupee tray and a paise tray, strips ruled into a hundred cells, a counting tray of value slots, a bill slip with a dotted line, a shop counter with a change tray, a multiplying frame under a row of things, and a till with a share mat.

Every note and coin shows its value in large figures and nothing else: no design, no picture, no lettering but the value. Every note is a plain paper rectangle and every coin a plain metal disc, all notes one size and one colour and all coins one size and one metal, so a value is read from its print and never from size or colour.

No coin below one rupee is drawn or named anywhere. Wherever paise are drawn rather than written, they are shaded cells on a rupee strip ruled into a hundred equal cells in ten blocks of ten, so a full strip is exactly one rupee. Nothing standing for paise is ever round.

Written money with paise is Rs, the rupees, a dot and two digits of paise, as Rs 96.75. Fewer than ten paise are written with a zero in the first place after the dot. A whole amount in running text is written with no dot, as Rs 43.

Column working always stands on a dotted line: every dot in a column sits on it, rupees to its left and paise to its right. In column working a whole-rupee amount carries two zeros in its paise column, drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit.

A hundred paise rolling up into one rupee is always shown moving, from the paise column into a small carry circle over the rupees, and a rupee broken into paise is always shown opening into a full strip of a hundred cells.
A rupees figure that goes down by one is struck through and the new figure written above it, never erased, so the break can be read afterwards.
The number of things in a product is a count. It stands in a box of its own beside the times sign, outside the rupees and paise columns, with no dot, and no cell exists for it under the paise.
Every answer slot carries its unit, rupees or things, printed beside the number.
A total, a change, a cost or an amount left is told apart by the slot or line it sits in first and by its colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit, a note, a coin, a cell or a slot the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, taken from the pictures, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. The rupees of every amount, the rupees column and the value printed on every note and coin are deep blue, and the paise of every amount, the paise column and every cell standing for paise are green. The dot between rupees and paise is vermilion in every tool, drawn as a clear round dot on the dotted line. A rupee carried from the paise, and a rupee broken into a hundred paise with the digits it rewrites, are amber. The change handed back, the money left and a remainder are reddish purple, so money coming back is never mistaken for a cost. A count of things, a number multiplied by, how many notes of one value or how many can be bought, is sky blue, because a count is never money. The two zeros in the paise column of a whole-rupee amount are grey, drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and never faded. Every play note is one plain pale blue and every play coin one plain steel, so a value is read from its print and never from its colour. All of that holds in greyscale, because a digit is told apart by the column it stands in, a carry by the circle it sits in and a count by the box beside the times sign, before any of them is told apart by colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Read the question card again. Is the answer rupees, or things?
voice.onNext: A new question. Say what the answer counts before you divide.
voice.opening: A till of rupees and a shelf of things. What is the question asking for?
voice.onFinish: Every cost of one found, every count of things given, and every rupee left kept.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any whole rupee amount and any price, with the mat, the lane and the table open.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: At the end of the chapter, after pairs have spent a purse of play money at a tuck shop price list and checked by multiplying back. The tool is what keeps the unit of every answer in front of the child, rupees or things, which a bare quotient on paper does not show.

answer_key.rule: When each thing costs the same, the cost of one is the total cost divided by the number of things, and it is money. The price of one ticket is the amount spent divided by the number of tickets, and the total spent adds the amounts spent, not one ticket from each row. How many things an amount buys is the money divided by the price of one, and the answer is a number of things. In such a division the remainder is the money left over, too little to buy one more. Every division in this chapter divides a whole number of rupees. Multiply back and add the money left to check. The chapter's six words mean this. Currency is the money a country uses, in notes and coins. A note is paper money and a coin is metal money. To buy is to pay money for something. A bill lists the things bought and their prices. Cost is the price to be paid.
answer_key.wrong: The share mat deals the money out again pile by pile, or the buy lane pays the price out again one thing at a time, while the answer slot lights its unit. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The total cost is shared equally among 6 lunch boxes, so divide 522 by 6.
52 tens divided by 6 is 8 tens, with 4 tens left, and 42 ones divided by 6 is 7.
So one lunch box costs Rs 87. Check: 6 times 87 is 522.
items.question: 6 lunch boxes cost Rs 522. What does one lunch box cost?
items.checkpoint: When each thing costs the same, the cost of one is the total cost divided by the number of things.
items.misconception: Multiplying 522 by 6, which gives the cost of 36 lunch boxes, not one.

steps: First row: 858 divided by 6 is 143, so one ticket costs Rs 143.
Second row: 560 divided by 8 is 70, so one ticket costs Rs 70.
The total spent adds the amounts spent: Rs 858 and Rs 560 make Rs 1418.
items.answer: Rs 143 and Rs 70 for one ticket, and Rs 1418 spent in all
items.question: A ticket table has two rows. In one, 6 tickets were bought for Rs 858. In the other, 8 tickets were bought for Rs 560. Find the price of one ticket in each row, and the total spent.
items.checkpoint: The price of one ticket is the amount spent divided by the tickets; the total spent adds what was spent.
items.misconception: Adding one ticket from each row, Rs 143 and Rs 70, and calling Rs 213 the total spent.

steps: Divide the money by the price of one: 1467 divided by 9.
14 hundreds gives 1 hundred with 5 left, 56 tens gives 6 tens with 2 left, and 27 ones gives 3.
So 163 notebooks can be bought. The answer is a number of notebooks, not rupees.
items.question: A notebook costs Rs 9. How many notebooks can be bought for Rs 1467?
items.checkpoint: How many can be bought is the money divided by the price of one, and the answer counts things.
items.misconception: Writing Rs 163, as if the answer were money.

steps: Divide the money by the price: 1597 divided by 6.
15 hundreds gives 2 with 3 left, 39 tens gives 6 with 3 left, and 37 ones gives 6 with 1 left.
So 266 pencils, with Rs 1 left, too little for one more. Check: 6 times 266 is 1596, and 1 more makes 1597.
items.question: Pencils cost Rs 6 each. How many can be bought for Rs 1597, and how much money is left?
items.checkpoint: The remainder is the money left over, too little to buy one more.
items.misconception: Dropping the Rs 1 left, or counting it as one more pencil.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: 5 caps cost Rs 465. What does one cap cost?
9 chairs cost Rs 3006. What does one chair cost?
4 tickets cost Rs 332. What is the price of one ticket?
A bill for 7 tickets shows Rs 861 spent. What is the cost of one ticket? Say what the bill lists and what cost means.
items.final_answer: Rs 123. The bill lists the things bought and their prices, and cost is the price to be paid, here for one ticket

items.question: A kite costs Rs 7. How many kites can be bought for Rs 1582?
items.final_answer: 226 kites, because 1582 divided by 7 is 226. The answer is a number of kites, not rupees

items.question: Erasers cost Rs 4 each. How many can be bought for Rs 150, and how much is left?
items.final_answer: 37 erasers, with Rs 2 left, because 4 times 37 is 148

items.question: A box holds 18 coins, with equal numbers of Rs 10, Rs 5 and Rs 2 coins. How much money is in the box?
items.final_answer: Rs 102. There are 6 coins of each kind, so Rs 60, Rs 30 and Rs 12

items.question: Juice packs cost Rs 12 each. How many can be bought for Rs 500, and how much money is left?
items.final_answer: 41 packs, with Rs 8 left, because 12 times 41 is 492

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: says what is known and what is asked
holds a whole number of rupees in notes and coins
splits an amount into equal piles, one for each thing
writes the same division in full beside the mat
holds tickets bought and amounts spent, with a blank price column and a total line
pays the price of one out again and again until too little is left
carries the unit asked for, rupees or things

teaching_notes: Run a tuck shop with a price list in whole rupees and a purse of play money for each pair before the tool is opened, and have them multiply back to check every answer. Then use the tool to keep the unit of each answer in view. Dividing a total cost by the number of things gives the cost of one, in rupees. Dividing money by a price gives how many can be bought, a number of things, and the remainder is money too little for one more. Every division in the chapter divides a whole number of rupees; none divides an amount with paise, and this tool claims nothing more. The closing ticket table asks for the price of one ticket in each row and then the total spent, which adds what was spent. The book's own answer labels each price with the buyer's name, but it is the price of one ticket. The vocabulary box asks for flashcards with definitions and never gives any, so give the plain meanings. Currency is the money a country uses, in notes and coins. A note is paper money and a coin is metal money. To buy is to pay money for something. A bill lists the things bought and their prices. Cost is the price to be paid. The self-assessment's first line, identifying notes and coins, is practised nowhere in the chapter; the Money Tray's first phase, which sorts them by value, is the nearest.
generation_prompt: Build a shop dividing tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. The working area is a shop counter with a till of whole-rupee notes and coins on the left, a shelf on the right, and a question card across the top saying what is known and what is asked. A share mat between them deals an amount of money into equal piles, one pile for each thing, while a division frame beside it writes the same division in full, bringing one digit down at a time. A ticket table can replace the mat: rows of tickets bought and amounts spent, a blank price column, and a total line under the amounts spent. A buy lane works the other way round: a price tag is set, and the till pays that price out again and again, one thing at a time onto the shelf, stopping when what is left is less than the price. The things bought stand in a counted row, and the rupees left stay in a tray labelled money left. An answer slot fixed down the right of the canvas carries the unit the question asks for, rupees or things, and a check control multiplies back and adds the money left. Every amount the till can hold is a whole number of rupees. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Share the total to find the cost of one. Divide the money by the price to find how many. The money left is the remainder. Say rupees or things in every answer.
